concept.name: Type I error
concept.definition: Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true - a false positive. Its probability is denoted alpha and is controlled by the chosen significance level of the test.
concept.intuition: It is declaring a lucky strategy to be skill: you concluded there is an edge when in truth there is none.
concept.mechanics: Setting the significance level alpha (commonly 0.05) caps the probability of a Type I error under the null at alpha: the null is rejected only when the test statistic falls in the extreme critical region, which happens with probability alpha when H0 holds.
concept.formula: alpha = P(reject H0 | H0 is true); by construction of the test, alpha equals the significance level.
concept.failure_modes: The nominal alpha holds per test: running many tests (signal mining across hundreds of strategies) multiplies false-positive chances far beyond alpha unless corrected. Model misspecification (wrong null distribution for fat-tailed returns) also breaks the guarantee that the true Type I rate equals the stated alpha.
concept.misconceptions: A Type I error is not 'the data were unlucky' after the fact - it is a property of the testing procedure, not of any single outcome. Nor does a small alpha eliminate false positives; it only caps their rate among true nulls.
concept.example: With alpha = 0.05, a backtest of a genuinely useless signal (H0: zero edge, true) will still produce a 'significant' t-statistic about 5% of the time - a Type I error that can launch a doomed strategy.
